title: Who is Assessment For?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that assessment is not primarily for parents or even students but for improving the curriculum. His thought experiment is that even perfect KS3 assessment would not move any student up a grade at GCSE, which depends on how well they have learned what was taught. He lists four more important jobs: improving the curriculum, ensuring students learn and remember what is taught, and finding out what still needs learning. His central move is to put assessment at the beginning of curriculum design, with intent dictating assessment tasks, which dictate knowledge, activities and sequencing, illustrated by how driving tests shape driving lessons. He then asks ChatGPT for ten writing tasks as a demonstration and challenges teachers to write better ones, suggesting fear of the GCSE is what holds curricula back.
points: Salles claims assessment's main purpose is to improve the curriculum, not to inform parents or produce grade gains.
He names four jobs of assessment: curriculum improvement, learning, remembering and diagnosing remaining gaps.
Assessment belongs at the start of curriculum planning, where intent determines the tasks, then knowledge and sequence.
The driving test analogy shows that define-the-assessment-first is how learning works outside school.
A ChatGPT-generated set of ten writing tasks is offered as a mirror, implying GCSE question types have narrowed writing curricula.
quotes: Imagine your assessment is completely meaningful at KS3. It’s the bee’s knees of assessment. How many students will go up a grade at KS4 as a consequence of how well you have assessmed them? None, I'd guess. They’ll go up a grade at GCSE based on how well they have learned what you’ve taught them. That will be the same, whether your assessment is the bee’s knees, or the bee’s backside.

However accurate your assessment at KS3, the student probably won't get a tutor until an adverse assessment in year 10 or 11. So, for me, in the best case scenario at KS3, informing parents, however accurately, will make no difference to how students do at GCSE.

For me the curriculum starts with the intent, which dictates the assessment tasks, which dictates the knowledge and skills taught, which dictates the activities in the curriculum and the sequencing of those.
The intent determines the assessment. The curriculum follows from that. It is obvious.

Assessment isn't something we put at the end of the curriculum, to see how well students have learned it. We put it right at the beginning of the curriculum to work out that it is the right curriculum.

If these were your assessment tasks, you would totally change your curriculum, wouldn’t you? But, you are a professional, passionate about your subject. You and your team could come up with 10 tasks which are even better than the average American on the internet, can’t you? What is stopping you? The fear of the GCSE.
